title: 10 Reasons Why Accessibility Teams Will Love Constellation (and your users will too)
summary: When people talk about digital accessibility, they often think about compliance checklists, audits, and regulations. Those things matter, but they're not the reason we're excited about accessibility in Constellation. The real goal is simple: Build experiences that work better for everyone. When we designed Constellation, accessibility wasn't treated as an add-on. It was considered from the beginning, baked into the design system, components, authoring experience, and platform capabilities. We wanted application teams to spend less time worrying about accessibility implementation details and more time solving business problems. The result? A platform that helps organizations create more inclusive applications while helping authors avoid many of the accessibility pitfalls that traditionally require specialized expertise. These ten examples highlight why moving to Constellation can be a game changer for both users and builders. #1 - Labels that never leave users behind Let's start with one of the most important building blocks of accessibility: labels. In Constellation, every field has a semantic relationship to a label. By default, labels are visible because clear, visible context benefits everyone. We understand that some organizations have specific design requirements, so label visibility can be adjusted when needed. Here's the important part: even when a visible label is hidden, the programmatic label remains available to assistive technologies. And because accessibility is as much about education as implementation, authors receive an accessibility warning when label visibility is removed. We're not preventing configuration choices, but we are making sure authors understand the impact of those choices. Accessibility shouldn't be accidental. Constellation helps make it intentional. #2 - Contrast checks built right into the authoring experience Choosing colors is fun. Choosing colors that everybody can read? Sometimes less fun. That's why Constellation helps identify contrast issues before they become usability problems. Authors are alerted when text and background color combinations may not provide sufficient contrast. We don't lock users into a rigid color palette. Instead, we provide guidance and visibility into potential issues so teams can make informed decisions. Think of it as a friendly accessibility coach sitting beside you during design. #3 - Color is great... but let's add meaning too Many organizations use color to highlight important information such as risk levels, performance metrics, or service issues. The challenge? Not everyone perceives color the same way. When authors create conditional formatting in Constellation, the experience encourages the addition of icons or other visual indicators alongside color. This ensures important information isn't communicated through color alone. Can authors remove the icon? Yes. Will Constellation remind them why that might create challenges for users? Also yes. Accessibility works best when meaning is reinforced in multiple ways. #4 - A live alert log that respects real workflows Imagine working in a busy contact center. You're speaking with a customer, reviewing case information, updating data, and receiving notifications all at the same time. Now imagine if you used a screen reader and try to keep up with every audible announcement happening during that interaction. That's why Constellation includes a live alert log that captures recent announcements for later review. Users don't have to worry about missing an important update. They can focus on the task at hand and retrieve recent announcements when they're ready. It's a small feature with a surprisingly large impact on productivity and usability. #5 - Full-screen tables for better focus If you've worked with enterprise applications, you've probably spent plenty of time staring at tables. Sometimes a table is just one piece of information on a crowded page. Other times, it's the page. Constellation allows users to expand tables into a full-screen experience, creating a cleaner, more focused environment for reviewing and interacting with data. Less distraction. More focus. This full-screen features is gradually being leveraged in all areas of the application. Sometimes accessibility isn't about adding something new. It's about removing unnecessary friction. #6 - Data entry tables that actually work For years we've heard the same request: "Can I enter data directly in a table?" Users love tables because they're familiar and efficient. The problem is that interactive tables are often incredibly difficult to make accessible. Constellation gave us the opportunity to rethink this pattern from the ground up. By aligning with established accessibility guidance and creating consistent interaction models, we've enabled support for rich interactions within tables, including links, buttons, dropdowns, radio buttons, checkboxes, rich text fields, and more. Enterprise applications need powerful data entry experiences. Now they can be powerful and accessible. #7 - Keyboard shortcuts that save time Screen reader users have long benefited from shortcuts that help them move quickly between page regions. We wondered: Why should they have all the fun? Constellation introduces keyboard shortcuts, such as F9 region navigation, that help keyboard users jump directly to important areas of a page without tabbing through every control. The result is faster navigation, reduced fatigue, and a more efficient experience for power users. Because accessibility improvements often turn into productivity improvements. #8 - Drag and drop for everyone Drag-and-drop experiences are undeniably cool. They're also notoriously difficult to make accessible. In Constellation, we didn't want accessibility to mean missing out on modern experiences. That's why keyboard-accessible alternatives are incorporated into drag-and-drop functionality. Users can move content using structured keyboard interactions and alternative selection methods rather than relying solely on a mouse. The best innovations are the ones everyone gets to use. #9 - Charts you can actually explore Charts are fantastic for presenting insights. Unfortunately, they're often terrible for accessibility. Constellation takes a different approach. Charts are navigable by keyboard and screen reader users, allowing individuals to move through chart content, understand the relationships being presented, and even explore the underlying data. Managers, analysts, supervisors, and team leads shouldn't have to choose between insights and accessibility. With Constellation, they don't. #10 - AI assistant: fewer tabs, faster answers (last but definitely not least) One of the biggest accessibility challenges in complex applications is navigation. Keyboard users may need to move through dozens of controls to reach the information they need. Screen reader users may need to explore large amounts of content sequentially. Constellation's AI Assistant changes that conversation. Instead of navigating through multiple screens, users can interact through a conversational interface to complete tasks, retrieve information, and find answers directly. Even better, users can choose the interaction method that works best for them, including voice-based interactions. The shortest path to accessibility is often the shortest path to accomplishing the task. The bigger story The most exciting thing about these features isn't any single capability. It's the philosophy behind them. Constellation was designed to help organizations create inclusive experiences at scale. Accessibility considerations are built into components, patterns, warnings, guidance, and interactions so application authors don't need to be accessibility experts to create significantly better user experiences. They're simply ten examples that demonstrate what happens when accessibility is considered from the start instead of adding at the end. And that's really the value of Constellation: helping teams build applications that more people can use, more efficiently, with less effort and fewer barriers. Because accessibility isn't a feature. It's a better way to build software.
body_markdown:
When people talk about digital accessibility, they often think about compliance checklists, audits, and regulations. Those things matter, but they're not the reason we're excited about accessibility in Constellation.


The real goal is simple: Build experiences that work better for everyone.


When we designed Constellation, accessibility wasn't treated as an add-on. It was considered from the beginning, baked into the design system, components, authoring experience, and platform capabilities. We wanted application teams to spend less time worrying about accessibility implementation details and more time solving business problems. The result? A platform that helps organizations create more inclusive applications while helping authors avoid many of the accessibility pitfalls that traditionally require specialized expertise.


These ten examples highlight why moving to Constellation can be a game changer for both users and builders.


## #1 - Labels that never leave users behind


Let's start with one of the most important building blocks of accessibility: labels.


In Constellation, every field has a semantic relationship to a label. By default, labels are visible because clear, visible context benefits everyone. We understand that some organizations have specific design requirements, so label visibility can be adjusted when needed.


Here's the important part: **even when a visible label is hidden, the programmatic label remains available** to assistive technologies. And because accessibility is as much about education as implementation, authors receive an accessibility warning when label visibility is removed. We're not preventing configuration choices, but we are making sure authors understand the impact of those choices. Accessibility shouldn't be accidental. Constellation helps make it intentional.


## #2 - Contrast checks built right into the authoring experience


Choosing colors is fun. Choosing colors that everybody can read? Sometimes less fun.


That's why Constellation **helps identify contrast issues before they become usability problems.** Authors are alerted when text and background color combinations may not provide sufficient contrast.


We don't lock users into a rigid color palette. Instead, we provide guidance and visibility into potential issues so teams can make informed decisions. Think of it as a friendly accessibility coach sitting beside you during design.


## #3 - Color is great... but let's add meaning too


Many organizations use color to highlight important information such as risk levels, performance metrics, or service issues. The challenge? Not everyone perceives color the same way.


When authors create conditional formatting in Constellation, the **experience encourages the addition of icons or other visual indicators** alongside color. This ensures important information isn't communicated through color alone. Can authors remove the icon? Yes. Will Constellation remind them why that might create challenges for users? Also yes.


Accessibility works best when meaning is reinforced in multiple ways.


## #4 - A live alert log that respects real workflows


Imagine working in a busy contact center. You're speaking with a customer, reviewing case information, updating data, and receiving notifications all at the same time. Now imagine if you used a screen reader and try to keep up with every audible announcement happening during that interaction.


That's why Constellation includes a **live alert log that captures recent announcements** for later review. Users don't have to worry about missing an important update. They can focus on the task at hand and retrieve recent announcements when they're ready.


It's a small feature with a surprisingly large impact on productivity and usability.


## #5 - Full-screen tables for better focus


If you've worked with enterprise applications, you've probably spent plenty of time staring at tables. Sometimes a table is just one piece of information on a crowded page. Other times, it's the page.


Constellation allows users to **expand tables into a full-screen experience** , creating a cleaner, more focused environment for reviewing and interacting with data. Less distraction. More focus. This full-screen features is gradually being leveraged in all areas of the application.


Sometimes accessibility isn't about adding something new. It's about removing unnecessary friction.


## #6 - Data entry tables that actually work


For years we've heard the same request: "Can I enter data directly in a table?" Users love tables because they're familiar and efficient. The problem is that interactive tables are often incredibly difficult to make accessible.


Constellation gave us the opportunity to rethink this pattern from the ground up. By aligning with established accessibility guidance and creating consistent interaction models, we've **enabled support for rich interactions within tables,** including links, buttons, dropdowns, radio buttons, checkboxes, rich text fields, and more.


Enterprise applications need powerful data entry experiences. Now they can be powerful and accessible.


## #7 - Keyboard shortcuts that save time


Screen reader users have long benefited from shortcuts that help them move quickly between page regions.


We wondered: Why should they have all the fun?


Constellation introduces keyboard shortcuts, such as F9 region navigation, that help keyboard users jump directly to important areas of a page without tabbing through every control. The result is faster navigation, reduced fatigue, and a more efficient experience for power users. Because accessibility improvements often turn into productivity improvements.


## #8 - Drag and drop for everyone


Drag-and-drop experiences are undeniably cool. They're also notoriously difficult to make accessible.


In Constellation, we didn't want accessibility to mean missing out on modern experiences. That's why **keyboard-accessible alternatives are incorporated** into drag-and-drop functionality. Users can move content using structured keyboard interactions and alternative selection methods rather than relying solely on a mouse.


The best innovations are the ones everyone gets to use.


## #9 - Charts you can actually explore


Charts are fantastic for presenting insights. Unfortunately, they're often terrible for accessibility.


Constellation takes a different approach. Charts are navigable by keyboard and screen reader users, allowing individuals to move through chart content, **understand the relationships being presented** , and even explore the underlying data.


Managers, analysts, supervisors, and team leads shouldn't have to choose between insights and accessibility. With Constellation, they don't.


## #10 - AI assistant: fewer tabs, faster answers (last but definitely not least)


One of the biggest accessibility challenges in complex applications is navigation. Keyboard users may need to move through dozens of controls to reach the information they need. Screen reader users may need to explore large amounts of content sequentially.


Constellation's AI Assistant changes that conversation. Instead of navigating through multiple screens, **users can interact through a conversational interface to complete tasks,** retrieve information, and find answers directly. Even better, users can choose the interaction method that works best for them, including voice-based interactions.


The shortest path to accessibility is often the shortest path to accomplishing the task.


## The bigger story


The most exciting thing about these features isn't any single capability. It's the philosophy behind them. **Constellation was designed to help organizations create inclusive experiences at scale** . Accessibility considerations are built into components, patterns, warnings, guidance, and interactions so application authors don't need to be accessibility experts to create significantly better user experiences. They're simply ten examples that demonstrate what happens when accessibility is considered from the start instead of adding at the end. And that's really the value of Constellation: helping teams build applications that more people can use, more efficiently, with less effort and fewer barriers.


Because accessibility isn't a feature. It's a better way to build software.
